passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against Babylon that Isaiah son of Amoz received’ (verse 1).

A banner is raised on a bare hill, and the LORD calls his warriors to carry out his wrath (verses 2-3). ‘Listen, a tumult on the mountains, like that of a great multitude’ (verse 4). Kingdoms are gathering. ‘The LORD of Hosts is mobilizing an army for war’ (verse 4). They come from faraway lands to destroy the whole country (verse 5).

‘Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near; it will come as destruction from the Almighty’ (verse 6). Every hand goes limp and every heart melts (verse 7). Terror and anguish seize them, and they writhe like a woman in labor (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 12 closed the first section of Isaiah with a song that sent God's praise out to the nations. Chapters 13 to 23 now turn to those nations in a series of oracles: Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Cush, Egypt, Edom, Arabia and Tyre, with a word to Jerusalem among them. The collection makes one claim: the God of little Judah rules every empire and city on its map.

A burden, massa in Hebrew, is a heavy word laid on the prophet to deliver. It begins with Babylon. In Isaiah's day Babylon was an ancient, revered city in southern Mesopotamia, usually under Assyrian control and often in revolt. A Chaldean leader, Merodach-baladan, seized its throne around 721 BC and again briefly around 703 BC, and in 689 BC Sennacherib captured and devastated it. A century after Isaiah, Babylon would become the empire that destroyed Jerusalem. By opening with Babylon, the book announces that the empire that will one day seem invincible stands under God's judgment.

The Day of the LORD is God's day of reckoning. Here it falls on the empire, not on God's people.
passages.later: Amos had warned his own people about the same day: ‘What will the Day of the LORD be for you? It will be darkness and not light’ (Amos 5:18). Joel says, ‘The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD’ (Joel 2:31).
passages.asks: The oracles against the nations begin with the empire that would one day crush Judah. Ask which powers in your world seem invincible to you. And ask what it means to believe they too stand under God's judgment.

passages.t: The Day of the LORD, and the pride of the ruthless
passages.happening:
The Day of the LORD is coming, ‘cruel, with fury and burning anger’ (verse 9), to make the earth a desolation and destroy its sinners. The stars and constellations will not give their light, the rising sun will be darkened, and the moon will not shine (verse 10).

‘I will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their iniquity. I will end the haughtiness of the arrogant and lay low the pride of the ruthless’ (verse 11). People will become scarcer than fine gold (verse 12). The heavens will tremble and the earth shake (verse 13). Like a hunted gazelle or sheep without a shepherd, each will flee to his own land (verse 14).

Verses 15 and 16 describe what happens to those caught in a fallen city: killed by the sword, their children killed before them, their houses looted and their wives raped. These notes name what the verses describe and do not quote them.
passages.hearers:
The darkened sun, moon and stars are the language prophets use for the collapse of a world order. When an empire falls, it is as if the lights of heaven go out. The oracle widens from Babylon to the whole world: God will humble the arrogant and the ruthless everywhere.

The cruelties of verses 15 and 16 are what ancient conquest actually did. Assyrian and Babylonian armies routinely committed such atrocities, and Babylon itself would do them to Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. The first hearers knew these things from their own wars and their neighbors'.
passages.later: Jesus uses the language of verse 10 for the end: ‘The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light’ (Matthew 24:29). And God later charges Babylon for its own cruelty to his people: ‘You showed them no mercy; even on the elderly you laid a most heavy yoke’ (Isaiah 47:6).
passages.hard:
How can a prophecy from God describe infants killed and wives raped?

These verses are among the hardest lines in the prophets, and the difficulty should not be softened. Several things help in reading them. The prophet is describing what ancient warfare actually did. Babylon would do the same to Jerusalem, and Lamentations and Psalm 137 grieve it. The oracle announces that the violence Babylon inflicted will return on it, not that God approves the soldiers' cruelty. Elsewhere Isaiah and the other prophets condemn the conquerors' brutality even when they serve as God's instruments (10:5-15; 47:6). Many interpreters add that the Bible speaks of God giving people over to the consequences of their deeds, working through human evil without being its author.

None of this makes the passage easy, and honest readers have always found it disturbing. Its disturbing force is part of its warning: when empires sow violence, they reap it. Nothing in it makes such violence anything but evil, then or now, and it gives no one a warrant to wish it on any people.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God promises to lay low the pride of the ruthless. Ask where you have admired ruthlessness because it seemed to work. And ask how you can grieve the suffering of the innocent in a city that deserved judgment.

passages.t: The Medes, and Babylon left to the jackals
passages.happening:
‘Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who have no regard for silver and no desire for gold’ (verse 17). They will have no mercy, even on children (verse 18).

‘And Babylon, the jewel of the kingdoms, the glory of the pride of the Chaldeans, will be overthrown by God like Sodom and Gomorrah’ (verse 19). ‘She will never be inhabited or settled from generation to generation’ (verse 20). No nomad will pitch a tent there, and no shepherd will rest a flock.

Desert creatures will lie down there, and howling creatures fill her houses. Ostriches and wild goats will live there (verse 21). ‘Hyenas will howl in her fortresses and jackals in her luxurious palaces. Babylon’s time is at hand, and her days will not be prolonged’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The Medes were an Iranian people east of Assyria. They were allies of Babylon in the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC, and their kingdom was absorbed by Cyrus the Persian around 550 BC. Cyrus's empire of the Medes and Persians took Babylon in 539 BC.

The oracle's setting and fulfillment are debated. Many critical scholars date the chapter to the exile in the sixth century BC, when Babylon ruled and the rising Medes and Persians were its obvious threat. Others, including many who hold that Isaiah wrote it, point to its eighth-century setting: Babylon was already a byword for pride, and Isaiah elsewhere foresees exile to Babylon. When Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC it fell with little fighting and remained a major city. Its decline was gradual: damaged in revolts under the Persians, it lost importance when the Seleucid rulers founded Seleucia on the Tigris around 300 BC, and it was largely deserted by the early centuries AD. Some readers see the prophecy fulfilled over that long decline.

The picture of a palace given over to jackals and hyenas was a common way of describing a city's complete ruin.
passages.later: Jeremiah says the same of Babylon: ‘The LORD has aroused the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because His plan is aimed at Babylon to destroy her’ (Jeremiah 51:11), and ‘desert creatures and hyenas will live there’ (Jeremiah 50:39).
passages.asks: Babylon, the jewel of the kingdoms, ends as a home for jackals. Ask what glory you are building that could end the same way. And ask what it means that the empire's fall took centuries, while the prophet saw it as one picture.
